Solutions/Pallet storage

Very Narrow-Aisle (VNA) Racking

Use warehouse height and narrower operating aisles with specialist handling equipment.

Discuss this system → Read the FAQs ↓

Overview

How it works

VNA storage reduces aisle footprint compared with conventional layouts. It requires coordinated engineering of rack geometry, floor tolerance, guidance, equipment selection and safe travel routes.

Typical applications

  • High-density logistics
  • Pharmaceutical distribution
  • Warehouses with expensive floor area

Benefits

Why choose it

01

Higher spatial efficiency

Allocate more of the available footprint to storage locations.

02

Vertical utilisation

Coordinate storage elevation with available clear height.

03

Structured traffic

Design around specialist turret or guided truck operations.

Engineering

Design considerations

Aisle width
Specific to the selected VNA truck and manufacturer criteria.
Operating height
Defined by truck lift reach, building and fire clearances.
Floor flatness
Validated against specialist equipment requirements.
Guidance method
Rail or wire guidance, if required by equipment.
Load rating
Approved through project-specific structural calculations.

Technical specifications are design considerations, not fixed certified performance values. Confirm claims with engineering and supplier data before deployment.

FAQs

Common questions

How does VNA racking save space?

It can reduce floor area allocated to aisles, allowing more rack locations in the same building envelope, subject to actual equipment and layout constraints.

Can standard forklifts operate in a VNA aisle?

VNA aisles usually need purpose-selected equipment; standard forklift compatibility must not be assumed.

Is special floor preparation necessary?

Floor flatness and levelness must be assessed against the selected VNA handling equipment and its guidance approach.

What determines the storage capacity?

Capacity follows the approved plan including pallet dimensions, available height, aisle and truck geometry, structural loads and operational constraints.
